activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Elijah had agreed to meet Marisol at the community garden because her mother said the house was too loud for studying, which was a subterfuge, since the real reason was that the tomatoes needed watering and Marisol's court-ordered community service had somehow become everyone's habit. She sat on an overturned bucket with a biology textbook open on her knees, glaring at a diagram the way she usually glared at the kale.

"Look at this," she said, jabbing the page. "They change one letter in the DNA. One. And then they say, and I quote, 'the resulting protein is unchanged.' Unchanged? How? If I change a letter in a recipe from 'bake' to 'cake,' I get a different sentence. If I change one brick in a wall, it's a different wall."

"Maybe it's a typo," Elijah offered, dragging a second bucket over. He was supposed to be learning this material himself, for a test on Monday, and being asked to explain it felt like being asked to juggle while drowning.

"It's in the textbook. Textbooks don't do typos, they do tragedy." She flipped the diagram toward him. "See? The codon went from one thing to another thing, and the amino acid is the same one. Same one, Elijah."

He leaned in. The garden hummed around them, somebody's wind chime doing its thin silver business, and for a moment he almost said he had no idea, which would have been honest but useless. Instead he said, "Okay, wait. Let me tell you the whole pipeline first, because I think the answer's in there somewhere, and if I get it wrong we can blame the textbook anyway."

"Proceed," said Marisol, saturnine as a gargoyle, arms folded over the bucket.

"So DNA gets copied into RNA. That's transcription. It's like, okay, this is going to sound dumb." He picked up a dry leaf and held it like a card. "DNA is the master recipe written in ink, and you don't want to get marinara on your only copy, so you photocopy it. The photocopy is RNA. Except the copier can't read one of the letters, so everywhere the DNA says T, the copy says U. It's not translating, exactly. It's more like transliterating, letter by letter, same words, different alphabet, like writing your name in Greek letters."

"Elijah becomes E-lambda-iota-alpha," Marisol said. "Still you, worse font."

"Exactly. Then translation, which is different. That's where the cell actually reads the RNA in groups of three letters, and every three-letter group is a codon, and every codon means one amino acid. Amino acids get chained together in order, and the chain folds up, and that's the protein. So the recipe metaphor kind of breaks, because it's less like baking and more like ordering at a restaurant in a language where some words are synonyms."

Marisol stopped glaring. "Synonyms."

"Wait," Elijah said, and the wait was real; he was flipping backward through his own memory of Monday's lecture, the codon chart the teacher had projected in colors like a plumbing diagram. "Wait, wait. Because several codons can code for the same amino acid." He said it slowly, testing the floorboards before putting his weight on them. "So if a mutation changes one base, one letter, sometimes the new codon still means the same amino acid as the old one. Same amino acid, same protein. Nothing changes."

Marisol looked at her diagram again, and her whole face did something complicated, like a door unlocking and a burglar alarm going off at the same time. "So it's a mutation that doesn't matter?"

"It matters and it doesn't," Elijah said. "The DNA changed, the RNA changed, but the finished protein comes out exactly the same. Those are called silent mutations."

"That's the most biologically dramatic term for 'no visible effect' I've ever heard," Marisol said. "Like a tree falling in a forest where all the trees are secretly the same tree."

"It's very quiet drama," Elijah agreed. "Meanwhile other mutations, the ones that do change the amino acid, those are loud. Those are the ones the test wants you to find."

They worked through her problem set in the smell of wet basil, Marisol reading codons aloud like lottery numbers, Elijah hovering over the chart. She got one wrong on purpose, he was almost sure, just to see if he'd catch it. He caught it. She grinned and gave him a tomato, the small ugly one, still warm.

"For the tutor," she said. "Silently accepted."

He turned it in his hand and said, "That's a subterfuge, that's a bribe," and ate it anyway, standing up, watering can already in the other hand, marching toward the kale.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
story:
Seth had been staring at the same two tables for forty minutes when Marcus finally looked over his shoulder and said, "You're overcomplicating it. Just find the customers with orders and subtract everybody else."

It was a fair suggestion, and Seth hated it. The tables sat side by side on Marcus's kitchen laptop, one listing customers with their IDs and names, the other listing orders with customer IDs and products. The assignment, from the online course they were both taking to pad their college applications, asked for something that sounded simple: which customers had never ordered anything. Mr. Alvarez, the instructor, had hinted that the answer involved a join, which was the whole point of the lesson, and Seth had decided he was not going to cheat the lesson by inventing a workaround.

"That's like finding everyone who didn't come to the party by counting who did," Seth said. "It works, but it isn't what he's asking."

Marcus rolled his eyes with theatrical patience. "It works, and it's eleven at night, and my mom's going to make us sequester ourselves in the basement if we keep arguing up here."

They had been friends since seventh grade, when Marcus had been the pugnacious kid who picked fights at recess and Seth had been the kid who watched him do it, cataloging the outcomes. Somewhere along the way Marcus had softened into a person who argued for sport rather than for blood, and Seth had discovered he liked being argued with, the way a musician likes a counterpoint, a second line running against his own that made both of them sharper. Tonight the counterpoint was getting on his nerves.

"Say it out loud," Marcus said. "Sometimes it helps. Say what you want the computer to do."

Seth rubbed his eyes and tried. "I want every customer from the customers table, and then, next to each one, their orders if they have any, and if they don't have any, I still want the customer. I just want the order columns to be empty."

He stopped. The sentence hung in the air between them, and something in it snagged. If he still wanted the customer even when there were no orders, then it wasn't the ordinary kind of join, the kind that matched rows and threw away the unmatched ones. It was a join that kept one side whole and let the other side go blank. He scrolled through the lesson notes until he found the phrase LEFT JOIN and read its description twice.

"Wait," he said. "I think the join itself can do the subtraction. You join everything, and then you look for the rows where the order side came back empty. The nothing shows up as an actual row instead of an absence."

Marcus leaned in, which he only did when something genuinely surprised him. "So the empty thing is a thing."

"The empty thing is a thing," Seth said, and typed it: a left join, then a condition checking whether the order's ID was null. He ran it. Two names came back, customers who had been sitting in the first table all along, quiet and orderless, invisible to the ordinary join. Seth felt a small, disproportionate thrill, the kind he associated with taking apart a clock as a kid and finding that one gear had been doing all the work.

He thought of that clock now, of the summer he was eleven and his grandfather had let him disassemble it on the porch, all the brass wheels laid out in a row on a towel, and had said only, "Notice which one isn't moving when it stops." He hadn't understood then that absence could be information. It seemed strange that a database language built by strangers decades before he was born should be teaching him the same lesson his grandfather had, but there it was.

Actually, that raised a question. "How do you even say it?" Seth asked. "S-Q-L, spelled out? Or sequel, like the movie?"

"Sequel," Marcus said immediately. "Definitely sequel."

"It's spelled S-Q-L."

"Doesn't matter. Everyone says sequel."

"Then why isn't it spelled that way?" Seth pulled out his phone and searched, and started laughing before he finished the first paragraph. "Because it was. It was first called SEQUEL. They developed it at IBM in the early 1970s. Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce."

Marcus took the phone and read it himself, frowning like a man being asked to concede a point he'd won by accident. "So I was right."

"You were right for no reason. That's not the same as being right."

Marcus held the phone a moment longer, then handed it back. Outside, a car swept past the kitchen window, its headlights dragging a slow rectangle of light across the ceiling. Seth looked at his two query results glowing on the screen, the two customers who had ordered nothing, and caught himself wondering what else he'd been passing over because it wasn't listed anywhere, what other absences were sitting in rows he'd never thought to join.

"Run it again," Marcus said. "I want to watch it work this time."

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
The laundromat closed at ten, and after the last customer left with her damp shirts over one arm, Audrey carried the traffic cones from behind the dryer and set them up in the parking lot. Her mother had bought the cones at a police auction, three dollars each, the same week Audrey turned fifteen and a half. Since then, three nights a week, while the final load of towels fermented in its own dampness because someone always forgot a load at closing, Audrey practiced parallel parking between the cones in her mother's Corolla.

The trouble was the angle. She kept finishing crooked, the rear of the car close to the curb and the front swinging wide, so that an imaginary car would have scraped its fender against the bumper of the imaginary car in front. Tonight she had done it five times, and each time she climbed out and looked at the geometry of her failure with her hands on her hips.

"You're turning too late," her mother said from the plastic chair by the door, where she sat counting the coin rolls. Her mother had driven delivery trucks for eleven years before the laundromat, and she did not rise from the chair to demonstrate anything. She believed, or said she believed, that Audrey should work it out herself, that driving was one of the few remaining meritocracies where the examiner didn't care how much money your family had or didn't have. Audrey thought this was partly a way of not admitting her mother couldn't afford actual lessons.

Audrey pulled forward alongside the front cone, the way the handbook showed, close and parallel, until her rear bumper sat just past it. She reversed, and this time she turned the wheel toward the curb immediately, watching the mirror. The car's nose swung out over the lane as the rear end came around. Then, when the cone appeared in the side window at the angle her mother had once marked with a piece of masking tape, she turned the wheel back the other way, away from the curb, and the car swung level into the space, straight, both cones still upright.

"Now that," her mother said, not looking up from the coins, "is how you do it."

She had been doing it backward without knowing. You went in from alongside the car in front, you turned toward the curb first, and then away, and the whole thing worked because of the order. Audrey sat in the parked car with her hands on the wheel and thought about how she had spent weeks trying to fix the angle by adjusting the second turn, when the problem had been the first one all along. Some errors you could only see from outside the mistake.

The highway was harder. On Saturday mornings they drove out to the ring road early, before traffic, and Audrey merged at sixty kilometers an hour with her jaw set. Her mother's method was to say nothing at all, which Audrey had learned to read as its own kind of instruction. The first time, she slowed at the end of the ramp and a delivery van honked. The second time she held her speed, found the gap, and slid into it, and her mother exhaled once, quietly, like a valve releasing.

The test was on a Tuesday. Audrey took the morning off school, which her history teacher would note, and which would cost her the extension on the essay she had already needed every day of. The examiner was a man with a clipboard and a gray mustache, and when he said "Parallel park at the next available space," her stomach dropped, because the space was small, smaller than the cones, and there was a real car in front of it with a bumper sticker about fishing.

She pulled alongside the car in front. She reversed, turning toward the curb, and when she judged the moment, she turned back away, and the car settled straight into the space with a hand's width on either side. The examiner made a mark on his clipboard and did not say anything, which she chose to believe was good.

She failed anyway, on the highway portion, for slowing below the flow of traffic during her second merge. The examiner said it kindly. In the parking lot afterward, her mother was leaning against the Corolla with her arms crossed, and when Audrey got in the passenger side and closed the door, neither of them spoke for a moment.

"Next month," her mother said, starting the engine. "The parallel parking was perfect."

"Small mercies," Audrey said, and watched the cones of the driving school lot across the street, where somebody else was setting up for the afternoon, sliding by the window as they pulled out.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Nicole had taped a grid of masking tape across the living room carpet, one square per meter of the imaginary stage, and by Tuesday evening the squares were already peeling at the corners. Her cousin Tasha and a boy from her chemistry class, Marcus, stood on the two downstage squares holding their scripts like shields. "From the top," Nicole said, sitting backward on the piano bench she'd dragged in as a director's chair. "You enter left, Marcus, you cross to her, and Tasha, you turn away before he finishes the line."

They moved like people wading through shallow water. Marcus read his lines with his eyes down, his feet planted as if the tape had glued him there, and Tasha kept drifting off her mark to glance at her script on the arm of the couch. Nicole stopped them four times in ten minutes. She had read that a director's real work was blocking, the architecture of movement, and she had believed it in the way you believe something you read at two in the morning: completely, and without any idea what it cost.

She had wanted this job since September, when the drama teacher announced that students could direct the winter one-acts and Nicole had raised her hand before she finished weighing it. Her mother had said, at the time, that directing was just telling people what to do with more politeness. Her father, who was impecunious that month and apologizing for it, had offered to buy her a director's megaphone as a joke, and she had laughed and not corrected him, because the truth was she didn't know yet what a director actually did.

"Tomorrow," she announced, when they had run the first scene six times, "is off-book." Tasha's head came up sharply. "What's that mean?" Marcus answered before Nicole could, because he had looked it up the night before, hoping to be spared. "An off-book rehearsal is one where we perform without scripts. Everything memorized." Tasha said nothing, but her thumb went to the corner of her pages and began worrying the paper, and Nicole pretended not to see it because she did not yet know what to do with what she was seeing.

That night she sat on the peeling tape grid alone and tried to introspect, which was a word her therapist used and which Nicole privately thought sounded like a machine part. What she found was not complicated: she had set the off-book date because a website said directors should, and she had enjoyed setting it, the small authority of the deadline, and she had never once asked whether Tasha could actually meet it. In chemistry that week they had started polymers, how a monomer was a single small unit that mattered only when it linked with others, in chains, and Nicole thought about how each rehearsal was supposed to work that way, each small unit clicking onto the next until the thing had shape. Her rehearsals were not linking. They were separate evenings of standing on tape.

The next evening Tasha made it through eleven lines and then stopped, mid-sentence, her face going stiff and remote, and said she was sorry, twice, and then a third time in a voice that made Marcus look at the carpet. Nicole felt the two directions pull at her like the tape pulling loose from the carpet in opposite corners. One was the deadline, the discipline, the argument that an audience would not hold scripts for anybody. The other was Tasha's thumb worrying the page corners last night, the apology now stacking up like something with weight.

"Okay," Nicole said. "New plan. Marcus, you're off-book, you stay off-book, you're ready. Tasha, we put the script on the chair. You can go to it when you need to, but every time you don't, we mark it, and Friday the chair moves to the hallway." Tasha looked at the chair, then at her. "That's still a deadline." "That's a staircase," Nicole said, though she was not sure it was, not sure it wasn't just a slower way to arrive at the same failure, and she let her face show that she wasn't sure, because hiding it felt like another thing she'd be directing rather than doing.

They ran the scene again. Marcus crossed to his mark, and this time he took Tasha's elbow as he spoke, a gesture Nicole had never given him, something he had found on his own, and Tasha turned away from him exactly on the beat, empty-handed, six lines before she needed the chair. They stood in the middle of the taped grid, both of them breathing a little hard, waiting to find out what came next. Nicole reached down and pressed one of the peeling corners flat against the carpet with the heel of her hand. "Again," she said. "From the top."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
The garage smelled of WD-40 and old sweat, and Devin had cleared a space on the workbench between a coffee can of screws and a bike wheel with no tire. He set down a battered notebook, open to a page of his own handwriting, and tapped it twice.

"Same problem as last night," Devin said. "Skater comes off the ledge at the park, going horizontal, four meters a second. Ledge is a meter and a quarter up. Where does he land?"

"In the gravel, probably," Nolan said. "That's where I landed."

"Nolan."

"I'm kidding. Sort of. I still have gravel in my elbow."

Devin was sixteen months older and phlegmatic about almost everything, including, apparently, his brother's failings. He slid the notebook across. Nolan looked at the page. There was a drawing of the ledge, an arrow, and then a long vertical drop of equations he did not follow.

"Here's what you told me yesterday," Nolan said. "You said split the velocity into pieces. Horizontal piece, vertical piece. And then what, they never talk to each other again?"

"They talk at the end. To get distance you need time of flight, and to get time of flight you use the vertical piece. But the whole flight, the horizontal piece just keeps going. Four meters a second at the lip, four meters a second when he lands."

"Nothing slows it down?"

Devin shook his head. "If you ignore air resistance, the horizontal velocity stays constant the whole flight, because no horizontal force is acting on it. Nothing's pushing it sideways. So it just goes."

"Gravity's not touching it?"

"Gravity pulls straight down. That's the vertical piece's problem."

Nolan sat down on an overturned milk crate and thought about that. It had a strange cleanliness to it. Down in the garage, with the door half open and the October light coming in flat and gray across the concrete, he could almost see the skater's arc, the horizontal arrow riding along it unchanged, calm, indifferent, while the vertical arrow stretched and stretched underneath.

"Okay," he said. "So how long is he in the air?"

"You did falling bodies three weeks ago."

"I did them badly."

"Do them well now."

Nolan took the pencil. He wrote one point two five equals one half g t squared, and then, because Devin was watching with the patience of a man waiting for a bus, he solved it. Half of nine point eight was four point nine. One point two five divided by four point nine, then the square root. He got about half a second. He said so.

"Okay," Devin said. "So how far does he go?"

Nolan's pencil stopped. The two halves of the problem sat there in front of him, the falling part and the going part, and for a moment he was back at the park, standing on that ledge in June, looking at the gravel and the board beneath his feet, and he had pushed off thinking about everything at once, speed and height and landing, and the thinking had gotten tangled and he had gone into the gravel with his arms out. He came out of the little reverie and found Devin waving a hand in front of his face.

"Hello."

"I'm computing."

"You're staring at a coffee can."

"They're the same thing." Nolan put the pencil down on the horizontal arrow. Four meters a second, the whole flight, because nothing horizontal was acting on it. Half a second in the air. "Four times half a second," he said. "Two meters. He lands two meters out."

"Which is?"

"Where I landed. Almost exactly. There's a scuff mark on the curb there, I've seen it."

"Congratulations," Devin said. "You can now predict your own injuries retroactively."

"Better than predicting them in advance, like you do."

Devin smiled at that, which for Devin was practically applause. He flipped to a fresh page and drew a new ledge, higher this time, with the takeoff at an angle, and Nolan's stomach dropped slightly, because an angle meant sines and cosines, meant the two pieces were tangled at the start even if they flew apart afterward.

"Angle of thirty degrees," Devin said. "Speed eight meters a second off the lip."

"So I have to split it first."

"You have to split it first."

Nolan wrote the sine and the cosine, and it occurred to him, halfway through, that he didn't actually know why the split worked, why the world was arranged so you could take one motion apart into two and then put them back together. He asked. Devin shrugged and said the man on the video said it does, and Nolan laughed, and wrote the numbers down anyway.

"Also," Devin said, "next time don't put your arms out when you fall. That's how wrists happen."

"You could have told me that in June."

"I was in Ohio in June."

"You could have sent a postcard. 'Dear Nolan, gravity pulls straight down. Love, Devin.'"

"Write the problem," Devin said, and stole the pencil back to underline the thirty degrees, twice, hard enough to dent the page.

story:
The kitchen table at Priya's house had been commandeer ed by four laptops, two bags of chips, and a poster board that was supposed to explain the immune response by Sunday. Jason set down his phone and looked at the diagram Dante had spent all Thursday night making, the one Dante was clearly proud of, the one with the arrows drawn in three colors and the title in bubble letters. It was also wrong. The diagram showed antibodies attacking the antigen directly, swallowing it like a Pac-Man, when what actually happened was that antibodies tagged the antigen so other cells could find it. It was the difference between a B and an A, maybe the difference between passing the unit at all.

"Pretty sick, right?" Dante said. He spun the marker between his fingers.

Nobody said anything. Priya was suddenly very interested in formatting the works cited page. Marcus opened his laptop wider, hiding half his face behind the screen.

"It's good," Priya said. "The colors are good."

Jason knew why nobody was saying it. He had almost said it himself, three weeks ago, when he'd messed up the solubility calculations in chem lab and Marcus had caught it but told him privately, later, in the hallway, in a voice like he was delivering bad news about a pet. Jason had spent the rest of that week feeling like the group's weakest link. But he'd also fixed the calculations, and the lab had come out fine, and somewhere in there he'd read something for his psych elective, a paragraph he'd screenshotted and never deleted. A researcher named Amy Edmondson, in 1999, had described something she called psychological safety: a team's shared belief that it was safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake. He'd thought it sounded soft at the time, a management word, the kind of thing adults put on posters. Now he wasn't sure it was soft at all. Their group had none of it, and here was the proof: four people sitting around a table, all seeing the same error, all pretending not to.

"It's good," Jason said, "but." Dante's shoulders went up half an inch. Jason kept going anyway. "The part where the antibody eats the antigen. That's not how it works. The antibody binds to it, like a tag. Then the macrophages come in. The rest of it, the layout, the color coding, that's the best thing anyone's made for this project."

Dante put the marker down. "You could've just said it looks good."

"I did say that. I also said the true part."

"Are you being facetious right now?" Dante said. "Because it's hard to tell."

"No. I mean the layout. I'd have done the whole thing in one color and it would've looked like a ransom note."

Marcus lowered his laptop a few degrees. "The binding thing is right," he said quietly. "I checked it too. I just didn't want to be the one."

"Didn't want to be the one to what?" Dante said.

"To make it a thing," Marcus said.

Priya pushed the works cited aside. "You mean like how nobody told me my slides had the wrong due date for two weeks."

"Nobody noticed," Jason said.

"Marcus noticed," Priya said. "He told me after."

Dante was quiet for a second, tapping the marker against the table. "So we all just do this. We all sit on it."

Jason pulled the screenshot up on his phone and slid it across the table. "Read this. I've had it saved for like a month." Dante read it, then read it again, then passed it to Priya without a word.

"Okay," Dante said finally. "Okay. So I fix the arrow." He uncapped the marker, hesitated over the diagram, and looked up. "But you're telling me how. Not just that it's wrong. Because I swear I read that section."

"The antibody's the label, not the teeth," Jason said. "Draw it like a flag stuck on the antigen, and the macrophage as the guy who follows the flag."

"A flag," Dante repeated. He drew it. It took him forty seconds, and it was obvious now, and it looked better than the original. He turned the board around. "Like that?"

"Exactly like that," Jason said.

Priya wrote something in the margin of her notes, and when Jason leaned over he saw it was just the date, 1999, circled twice, like a thing worth remembering. Marcus finally closed the laptop all the way.

"So the deal is," Dante said, capping the marker, "next time one of us screws up, we just say it. Out loud. At the table."

"Out loud," Priya said. "At the table."

"Even me," Marcus said.

Dante pointed the marker at him. "Especially you."

"Pass the chips," Jason said, and Marcus threw the bag across the table without looking up.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Matthew got the assignment on a Tuesday, fourth period, in the drama room that smelled like dust and the glue from last semester's set pieces. Write a ten-minute play about a moment from your own life, the handout said. Stage it. He had never written a play, only short stories for English, and even those had mostly been about characters he invented so that no one could ask him whether any of it was true.

He wrote about the afternoon his sister Beatrice had her allergy testing, because it was the one afternoon he could remember in detail: the waiting room, the numbered grid drawn in pen on her back, the doctor saying the word antigen as though it explained something, and their mother texting their father, who did not answer. Matthew put the unanswered text in the play as a real letter, because the teacher had said plays are spoken things and a phone screen is hard to stage. So the mother writes a letter in scene one and sets it on the table, and in the rest of the play nobody mentions it again.

On Thursday there was a table read in the library at lunch. Daniel read the father, Priya read the mother, and a girl named Oyelaran who Matthew barely knew read Beatrice, pronouncing the medical vocabulary better than anyone. They went through it once, and then Daniel leaned back in his chair and tapped the page.

"Okay, but the letter," Daniel said. "You spend like half a page on her writing it in scene one. And then nothing. Why is it there?"

"Because that's what happened. She wrote to him and he didn't answer."

"Sure, but on a stage it reads like a clue. Like it's going to come back." Priya nodded at that. Daniel shrugged. "There's a principle called Chekhov's gun, from the playwright Anton Chekhov. Anything clearly shown on stage early should matter later in the play." He said it the way he said most things, as though quoting something he'd read on his phone at two in the morning.

Matthew argued for a minute. The silence was the point, he said. The father's absence wasn't a prop; putting a payoff in would reify it into a plot device, an object with a function, when in real life the letter just sat there useless. Priya said that might be true in life but an audience watches a stage, and a stage is not life, it's a small bright box where everything visible is a promise. Matthew said that sounded like a poster. Daniel ate his sandwich.

He went home and thought about it while doing his biology homework, which that week was about immune response, and he noticed that he liked the word antigen because it named a thing by what it provoked rather than what it was. Then he noticed he was avoiding the actual problem by finding it interesting. He sat at the kitchen table until eleven and rewrote the ending twice. In the first version, the father arrives in the last scene and reads the letter aloud. That felt false, a machine for delivering feeling. In the second version, Beatrice, waiting for her results, folds the letter into a paper boat and sails it on the sink in the exam room's bathroom, and the mother watches from the door and doesn't stop her. That felt closer to the actual afternoon, which Matthew now admitted he had been tidying.

But he kept the second version for a doctrinaire reason, he told himself, not just an emotional one: the letter now mattered later without explaining itself. The promise got paid without being cashed. He could defend it to Daniel. He practiced defending it to Daniel in the shower.

At the performance, in the black box theater with folding chairs and a card table borrowed from the front office, Oyelaran was very good. When she sailed the boat, somebody in the second row made a small sound, and the room went quiet in a way that felt like the play had landed. Afterward the teacher took him aside in the corridor and said the ending worked, that the paper boat had earned its moment.

Daniel found him by the water fountain. "So you fixed the letter," he said.

"I made it matter later," Matthew said. "It comes back as the boat."

"Right," Daniel said. "Only now the boat's the thing that doesn't come back." He was grinning a little. "You spend the whole last scene on it and then it's gone. Tomorrow someone's going to ask you what happened to the boat."

Behind them, the stage manager was striking the set, and Matthew watched her pick up the paper boat from the sink prop, flatten it with one hand, and drop it into the recycling bin with the programs.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
The community garden on Fell Street had gone to half weeds by August, and Robert had taken the onion bed because nobody else wanted it. He knelt there on Saturdays not because he loved onions but because the plot was quiet, and quiet places to study were scarce in his house, where his younger brothers treated every hallway as a racetrack. That Saturday he had his biology textbook open on the flattened cardboard between the rows, and he was losing an argument with a diagram that showed a long ladder curling like a ribbon.

The problem was simple and enormous. On Monday he had to explain, out loud, in front of the whole senior class, how DNA gets copied and how it becomes protein, and the textbook kept dissolving into arrows and labels the moment he looked away from them. RNA polymerase, messenger RNA, ribosomes, codons. He could recite the words. He could not make them mean anything, and Mrs. Okafor had been clear that reciting would not pass.

A shadow fell across the page. Dana from the next plot stood at the fence with a watering can, watching him with the particular amusement of someone who has caught a neighbor talking to an onion. Dana was garrulous in a way that filled whole afternoons, and Robert usually enjoyed it, but today he braced for a monologue about tomatoes.

"You look like the book insulted you," Dana said.

"It did." He turned the diagram toward her. "I have to explain this Monday. Transcription and translation. How DNA becomes protein. And I understand exactly none of it."

Dana set the can down and climbed the low fence, which was against the posted rules, and settled onto the cardboard beside him. She was studying to be a nurse, and had failed chemistry once before passing it, a fact she mentioned often and without shame. "Explain it to me, then. I'll tell you when you lose me."

He started, badly, with the ladder again. "So this is DNA, the double helix. Two strands, and the rungs are base pairs. And to copy it..." He stopped. The arrows on the page pointed at a blobby shape labeled helicase, but the blob told him nothing.

Dana was quiet for a moment, which was unusual. Then she reached for the zipper of her jacket and pulled it down slowly, the teeth separating two by two, a small sound like tearing paper. The jacket fell open into two halves.

"Okay," she said. "Do that with your hands. Show me."

Robert put the book down. He held his two hands flat together, fingers interlaced, then slid them apart like the jacket opening. "Before DNA can be copied," he said, mostly to himself, "it has to open. Something has to unzip it." He looked at the diagram again, at the blob, at the little marks where the rungs came apart. The label read helicase. He found it in the text, and there it was, in one sentence he had read four times without seeing: helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.

"That," he said. "That's the zipper. Helicase. It breaks the hydrogen bonds, the little things holding the base pairs together, and the two strands come apart." He pulled his hands apart again, farther this time, and something in his chest loosened the same way. "It's not magic. It's a jacket."

"Congratulations," Dana said. "You have now explained one percent of it."

"One percent that the rest hangs on." He was already moving, talking faster, pointing at each strand of his open hands in turn. "Because now you've got two single strands, and each one is a template. Free nucleotides, the little monomers, float in and pair up along each strand, and you get two copies." He paused. "I think that part is copying, actually, replication, which is separate from what I have to present. But it's the same opening move."

Dana pulled her jacket closed again, zipping it slowly, and he laughed, because that was the copy, two halves sealed into two wholes. He found the RNA polymerase arrow next, and now that the zipper was in his head, the rest began to arrange itself. The DNA opens the same way, one short stretch, and RNA polymerase reads along one strand, building a messenger RNA copy, a transcript, which then travels out of the nucleus to a ribosome, where the sequence gets read in threes and each three-letter word calls in a specific amino acid, and the amino acids link into a chain that folds into a protein. He stumbled at the ribosome, tried again, used the garden itself: the transcript was like a recipe card carried from the kitchen to the potting shed, and the ribosome was the gardener who read it and assembled the plants, one monomer at a time, until a whole protein stood where there had been only instructions.

"That last part was bad," Dana said, "but I followed it anyway."

He wrote it out in the dirt with a stick, the four steps, then wiped it clean with his palm and did it again from memory. Twice the order scrambled, and he sat back on his heels and stared at the onions until it unscrambled. He was aware that he did not fully understand it, that somewhere under the words were machines he could not picture, and that on Monday someone might ask why the hydrogen bonds specifically, and he would have to say he didn't know yet. That was tolerable in a way it had not been that morning. Not knowing had a shape now, and a place in the sequence, like a weed in a bed that had been mapped.

Mrs. Okafor's rubric wanted diagrams. Robert pulled his notebook from his backpack, found a clean page, and drew two jagged lines like the teeth of a zipper, with a fat blob riding between them and the words hydrogen bonds written along the rungs that were coming apart. He labeled the blob, printing carefully, HELICASE, and underlined it twice. Dana leaned over his shoulder, nodding as though approving a seedling.

"That's actually not terrible," she said. "For an onion bed."

He turned the notebook flat so the sun fell full on it, took out his phone, and started recording himself, speaking the first sentence out loud: "Before anything else can happen, an enzyme called helicase unzips the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs." His voice cracked on the second word, and he started over.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
story:
Tyson arrived at the community centre early, before the folding chairs had even been unlocked from the storage closet, because he had drawn the harder side. Mr. Ruiz, who ran the mock court program from a card table by the vending machines, had assigned each student a Supreme Court case and then flipped a coin to decide which side they would argue first. Tyson's case involved a speech, and his coin had come up for the speaker, which meant he had to defend a man everyone in the room would want to see punished.

The case file was thin on purpose. A man had stood on the steps of a county courthouse and told an angry crowd that a certain judge deserved to be dragged out of his chambers. Nothing had happened afterward; the crowd had dispersed, muttering, and the man had been charged under a state law against advocating violence. Tyson read the file twice on the bus, then a third time at the card table, and the argument for the speaker would not come. He kept writing openings and crossing them out, and the crossings-out accumulated until the margin of his page looked like a fence, something impermeable between him and the position he was supposed to hold.

A girl named Priya sat down across from him with her own folder. She had the same case, opposite coin. "You look like you're losing already," she said.

"I don't know how to defend him without defending the speech," Tyson said.

"That's the whole problem, isn't it." She slid a printed case across the table. "Brandenburg versus Ohio. My dad printed it from the library. Nineteen sixty-nine." She tapped the page with one finger. "The Court held that advocating force can be punished only if it's directed to inciting imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action."

Tyson read it, and read it again. The sentence had a shape, like a small machine, and each part had to be present or the machine would not run. Directed. Inciting. Imminent. Likely. He copied the four words onto his palm with a pen because he did not want to keep asking to look.

"You can have the copy," Priya said. "I already know it. I'm the state, so I get to say the crowd was one bad second away from dragging that judge out."

"Was it, though?" Tyson asked, but not to challenge her; he was asking himself, and she seemed to understand, because she shrugged and went to set up chairs.

By the time the other students filed in, twelve of them plus Mr. Ruiz with his clipboard, Tyson had found the seam in his own reluctance. When his turn came, he stood at the front and told the mock court that the question was not whether the speech was ugly, because it was. "The question," he said, "is whether it was directed to inciting imminent lawless action and likely to produce such action. He said the judge deserved it. He didn't say do it now. He didn't point at the door." He could feel the room wanting to argue with him, and he made himself keep going. "If we punish him for the wanting, not the inciting, then we don't have a standard anymore, we have whatever the majority feels that day. That's not a court. That's a despot with a gavel."

Priya cross-examined him hard, and well. She argued the crowd was seething, that imminence could be measured in temperature rather than minutes, and Tyson admitted under questioning that the line between a heated crowd and a dangerous one was not a line he could draw with a ruler. He said the standard was the best one he had, not a perfect one, and that he would rather protect ugly speech with a narrow rule than hand the state a blank check. Mr. Ruiz wrote something long on his clipboard and did not say what.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Priya caught up with him at the bike rack. "Ruiz flips the coins again next month," she said. "Same case, reversed. You'll argue for the state."

"Then I'll have to beat my own argument," Tyson said.

She smiled and zipped her folder into her backpack. "Good luck," she said. "It sounded pretty convincing to me." She pushed her bike toward the gate, and Tyson stood there with the case copy still in his hand, the four words inked on his palm, realizing he would spend the next month trying to exonerate exactly the argument he had just worked so hard to tear down.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
story:
The assignment had been posted on Thursday and was due at midnight on Sunday: implement a binary search, and in the comments of the code, explain in his own words why it beat a linear search when the data was sorted. Maxime had opened his laptop at the kitchen table on Saturday afternoon, written two lines, and closed it again. Now it was Sunday evening, and his grandfather was due for dinner at six, which left him roughly five hours if he wanted any sleep before his eight a.m. French exam.

Pépère arrived at six on the dot, as he always did, carrying a paper sack of pecans from the market on Rue Sherbrooke. He kissed Maxime's mother on both cheeks, settled into the chair at the head of the table, and watched Maxime push a textbook into his bag. "You have the face of a boy doing two things at once and doing neither."

"I have an assignment."

"After dinner," Maxime's mother said, and put the stew down.

It was Pépère who proposed the game, while the dishes were still being cleared. He took a napkin and a pen from his jacket, wrote the numbers 1 through 100 in a long uneven column, and said he was thinking of one of them. Maxime could ask if it was higher or lower, and each question had to be a whole number, a real guess. First to finish their potatoes had the advantage of choosing who guessed, and since Maxime had finished first, Pépère guessed.

Pépère began with 7. Higher. Then 12. Higher. Then 19, then 26, then 44, then 61, then 63, then 64, and it was 64, but only after eight questions, and Maxime counted them aloud as they went. When it was Maxime's turn, he asked 50. Lower. He asked 25. Higher. Then 37, then 43, then 46, then 48, then 49, and it was 49, seven questions exactly. They played four more rounds. Pépère guessed in nine, in eleven, once in six and once in twelve. Maxime never went past seven. After the fifth round Pépère set down the pen and said, "You are doing something."

"I'm cutting it in half."

From where she stood at the sink, Maxime's grandmother had been watching the last three games without comment. She had watched this boy grow up in her kitchen, and she knew his particular talent, which was not brilliance exactly but a kind of patience, the same patience he'd had at seven years old with a thousand-piece puzzle of a lighthouse. Her husband did not have it. He guessed the way he did everything, early and often and by feel. She dried her hands and said, "He always picks the middle, that one. You could pick 5 and 95 all night and he'd still get there before you."

"But why seven?" Pépère said. "Why not eight?"

"It just never takes more than seven," Maxime said. "I don't lose."

Pépère was quiet for a moment. Earlier that afternoon, before dinner, he had fallen asleep in the armchair by the window with the newspaper folded on his chest, and the somnolence of that nap still hung on him, making him slower to argue than usual. He looked at the napkin, at the long column of numbers, at the small torn places where the pen had pressed too hard. Then he took a second napkin and drew a line down the middle, and another, dividing the column again and again the way Maxime had divided it aloud, until the paper looked like the ribs of a fan. "Like this," he said. "You are not guessing at all. You are eliminating."

"That's binary search," Maxime said, mostly to himself. He had read the word three days ago on the assignment page and had not thought of it since, because he had been trying to compartmentalize, keeping the game at the table and the code on his laptop in two separate rooms of his head. They had not stayed separate. The stew, the pecans, his grandfather's slow tallying on his fingers, all of it was suddenly the same problem wearing different clothes.

He thought of one particular evening years ago, the winter he was nine. He had been looking up "stalactite" in the enormous dictionary that lived on the stand in the hallway, flipping from the front, and after ten minutes of turning pages Pépère had come down the stairs and shown him something different: open the book near the middle, look at the guide word, decide which half to keep. Maxime had forgotten it completely until now, but there it was, his grandfather's finger tapping the top edge of a page in the S's, saying, "You throw away half the book every time you choose." Pépère had known the trick all along and had never named it. He had simply used it and then guessed at numbers the way other men do, by birthday and by feel.

"Your mother says the computer thing is due tonight," his grandmother said.

Maxime got his laptop from his bag and opened it at the cleared end of the table. He typed while they watched, Pépère leaning forward with his forearms on the tablecloth. The low index, the high index, the middle, the comparison, the halving. It took him twenty minutes. In the comments, where the assignment asked him to explain why this beat checking every element one by one, he deleted his formal first draft and wrote instead: A sorted list can be halved like the numbers 1 to 100 in a guessing game. Picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses. A linear search might have to look at all of them. He read it over twice. There were things he was still unsure of, edge cases he hadn't tested, off-by-one errors that might be sleeping in the code, and he said so out loud, and Pépère said that was honest of him, and his grandmother said, "He is perspicacious, your grandfather means, when he isn't being lazy."

"Watch this," Maxime said. He ran the tests, all eleven of them, and leaned back so they could both see the screen.

Every one came back green, and Pépère reached across and turned the laptop slightly toward himself, squinting at the numbers as if checking for a trick.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
story:
The library's third-floor carrels were supposed to be silent, but Chloe had learned that silence was negotiable if you sat near the window and nobody came up before dinner. She had four days to build a presentation on greenhouse gases for Mr. Okafor's seminar, and the problem was not that she lacked material. The problem was that she kept finding graphs and forgetting where they came from, which mattered, because Okafor had a habit of asking, "And who measured this?" in the tone of a man checking receipts.

She had the science more or less in hand. Molecules like carbon dioxide absorb the infrared radiation the earth's surface gives off and re-emit it, some of it back downward, so the atmosphere holds heat the way a blanket holds warmth. She could picture it. What she could not picture was the graph everyone used, that sawtooth line climbing and climbing, and she had written in her notes only "famous CO2 graph, who??" with three question marks, as though the punctuation might summon an answer.

Her friend Priya found her there at five, dropped her bag, and stole half of Chloe's granola bar without asking, which was their arrangement. Priya was pre-med and treated Chloe's environmental science assignments as spectator sport. "How's the apocalypse going?"

"It's going," Chloe said. "I can explain the physics fine. It's the provenance that's killing me. Every source shows this curve and nobody says who drew it. Was it a lab? A satellite? Some guy with a notebook?"

"Some guy with a notebook," Priya said, with the certainty of someone who had no idea. "That's how everything was done before satellites. Find the guy."

Chloe wanted to preempt the moment on Friday when Okafor would ask his question and she would have nothing, so she kept digging. The station, she discovered after a wrong turn through a blog that called climate scientists bellicose and a second wrong turn through a site that wouldn't load, was in Hawaii. Not on a beach, which would have been the sensible place for a tropical vacation, but on a volcano, high up where the air was supposed to be clean. An institution in California had sent someone to start taking regular carbon dioxide measurements there in March 1958, and the graph those measurements produced had a name. She sat back. She had expected a committee, decades of funding meetings, at minimum a satellite. Instead there was one man on a mountain, counting molecules.

On Friday the seminar room smelled like the radiator and someone's instant noodles. Chloe went third, after a boy who read his slides verbatim in a monotone that tested the class's collective clemency toward him; even Okafor stopped saying "good" and started saying "hm." When Chloe's turn came, she put up the sawtooth curve full-screen and let it sit there for a second before speaking, which she had learned from watching presenters she admired.

"Everyone has seen this," she said. "It's in textbooks, in the news, on posters. The physics behind it is simple enough to be unfair: carbon dioxide absorbs the infrared the earth radiates and sends part of it back down, so the atmosphere traps heat. What nobody tells you is where the line comes from." She clicked to her second slide, a photograph of a bare volcanic slope under a wide sky. "A scientist named Charles David Keeling, from the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, began regular carbon dioxide measurements on Mauna Loa in Hawaii in March 1958. The measurements are still going, and the graph they produce is called the Keeling Curve."

Okafor looked up from his laptop, which was his version of applause. Someone in the back, the boy with the slides, raised his hand. "Wait," he said. "So one guy just... went up a volcano in 1958 and started measuring?"

"Basically, yeah," Chloe said.

"And we're still using his numbers?"

"The station is. That's the point of measuring something regularly for a long time. You can't get the curve any other way."

She talked through the rest of it, the sawtooth explained, the wobble in the line that she let them notice on their own before she named it, and when she finished Okafor asked only one question, which was whether she thought a single long dataset could change a person's mind. She said she honestly didn't know; she thought people changed their minds slowly, the way the line rose, and that a graph could be true and still sit there unanswered. She said that felt like the real uncertainty to her, not the measurements, and Okafor wrote something down, which she chose to interpret favorably.

Afterward, packing up, Priya appeared in the doorway with two coffees, one held out. "You were good. Very dignified."

"I panicked internally the whole time."

"Didn't show." Priya sipped her coffee. "So what was the guy's name again? Keebler?"

"Keeling," Chloe said, and hauled her bag onto her shoulder, and they walked out past the radiator and the empty seminar room, down the stairs and into the gray afternoon, where Priya asked her to explain the volcano thing one more time, slowly, because she hadn't been listening the first time and now she needed it for a party conversation she was planning to have on Saturday.

story:
Austin had claimed the table by the periodicals because it had the good lamp, and because Ms. Ferreira's assignment terrified him enough that he wanted witnesses. Apply one critical lens to a passage from a classic, she had written on the board, and be ready to defend it. He had chosen the opening of Pride and Prejudice, mostly because it was short, and he had spent twenty minutes staring at the sentence about a rich man wanting a wife before writing anything at all.

"You look like you're defusing something," said Priya, dropping her backpack on the chair across from him. She was in his class and had opinions about everything, which was either useful or dangerous.

"Marxist lens," he said. "Watch me try." He read aloud, half whispering, the part where Mrs. Bennet exhorts her husband to visit Mr. Bingley. "Okay. So marriage here is basically a transaction. The Bennets don't have sons, so the daughters have to convert themselves into money. The whole plot is people trying to move up a stratum, and the novel makes that feel like romance." He tapped his pen against the page. "It's not even hidden. Austen says it on page one."

"So write that," Priya said, peeling an orange in flat spirals, careless of the noxious smell of the peel filling the space between them. "Done. Go home."

But Austin didn't move. "It's the 'basically' that bothers me," he said. "I keep making it sound like Austen is tricking us, like the feelings are fake and the money is real. Except Elizabeth turns down Mr. Collins, who is the money. And she turns down Darcy the first time. If it's all economics, why does the novel reward her for refusing the economics?"

Priya considered this, or considered her orange. "Maybe that's the argument," she said. "The book lets a woman refuse, but only so she can be rewarded with a bigger prize. Like the system absorbing the criticism and selling it back."

Austin wrote refusing the economics? and then crossed it out, because it reified the exact thing he wasn't sure of: it turned a hunch into a fixed object, a little statue of an idea he could set on the shelf and stop questioning. He flipped the novel shut and opened his notebook to a blank page instead, drawing two columns, one headed money, one headed rooms, though he wasn't sure yet why the second word had come to him.

At the reference desk, a cart of returns waited to be shelved, and on top of it sat a slim book with a plain cover, A Room of One's Own, Virginia Woolf, 1929. He recognized the name from a list Ms. Ferreira had passed around, a supplement, she'd called it. He picked it up because the title matched the word in his column, which felt less like coincidence than like the library quietly eavesdropping on him.

He read standing up, one elbow on the cart. Woolf argued that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction. Austin read the line twice, then carried the book back to the periodicals table and set it next to Pride and Prejudice like a witness taking the stand.

"Listen," he said. "Woolf, 1929. A woman needs money and a room of her own to write fiction. Austen wrote this novel in a house full of people, at a little table, hiding the pages when anyone came in. That's a room that isn't her own." He paused, hearing himself. "So maybe my two columns aren't opposites. The marriage market and the writing are the same question. Who gets the money, who gets the room."

Priya had stopped eating. "So your Marxist lens," she said slowly, "and whatever you're doing now with Woolf, they're pointing at the same thing from two sides."

"That's what I don't know," Austin admitted, and it surprised him how good it felt to say it. For an hour he had wanted a single clean argument, something he could hand in like a key. Now he wanted the mess. He pulled the assignment sheet from his folder and, at the top, where it asked for his chosen lens, he wrote Marxist, then added in smaller letters, complicated by feminist critique, unresolved. It was the first time he had ever put the word unresolved on schoolwork, and he sat looking at it while the lamp hummed.

The library announcement crackled overhead, fifteen minutes to closing. Priya stacked her orange peels on a napkin and stood, and Austin slid both books into his backpack, Woolf checked out under his new card, Austen already his. At the door she held it open for him and said, "You know you just invented twice the work for yourself." Austin zipped the bag against the cold outside and said, "I know." He stepped past her onto the sidewalk, where the streetlights had just come on, one by one, all down the block.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
story:
Leo set the tripod between two roots where the trail widened, framing the creek so the water crossed the corner of the shot. He had forty-one minutes of footage and no video, because every time he started explaining transcription, his voice went flat and he stopped, and the takes piled up in the app's timeline like evidence against him. Monday was the retake. Priya had missed the unit entirely in the spring, which was why they had agreed to meet here instead of at the library, where the silence made him too aware of being watched. He pressed record.

"Okay. DNA is the recipe, but it stays locked in the nucleus, so the cell copies the gene into RNA. That's transcription." He heard his own voice on the small speaker, tinny and unconvinced. He dragged the clip to the trash. On the next take he moved to the footbridge and let the water run under his sentence, and the take was better until a dog crossed behind him and he laughed, and that clip went into the trash too.

"You're deleting yourself," Priya said from the bench where she sat with her knees drawn up, watching him scroll. She had a biology textbook open on her lap but hadn't turned a page since they arrived.

"I'm deleting the bad versions of myself."

"Feels like you're deleting most of yourself."

He half smiled and kept scrubbing through the timeline, and then he stopped. The app showed the clips as colored blocks on a track, and between the good ones sat short segments he had flagged to cut, the pauses, the false starts, the sentence where he said translation when he meant transcription. He pinched one out, and the two good blocks slid together and the sentence closed over the gap seamlessly. His heart gave a small palpitate, the way it did when a lock turned.

"Priya. Look at this." He held the phone out. "This is it. This is the part I couldn't remember." He pointed at the track. "The cell copies the gene, and the new RNA has junk in it, stretches that don't code for anything. In plant and animal cells, those get cut out. They're called introns." He tapped the block he had removed. "The parts that stay, the good takes, are called exons, and they get spliced together before the messenger RNA ever leaves the nucleus. So what arrives out there," he tipped his chin at the creek, at the water flowing away under the bridge, "is only the finished message."

Priya looked at the screen, then at him, and he could see the thing land in her face, the way it had landed in his. "So the cell edits itself before it sends anything out."

"Before it leaves the nucleus. Only the cut version goes out."

"And you just figured that out by deleting yourself."

"I figured it out by keeping the good takes."

She was quiet for a moment, which was like her, and then she closed the textbook without marking the page. "Leo, I have to tell you something, and I've been obdurate about it, which was stupid. I'm not taking the retake. I withdrew yesterday. My mom's job moved to Tucson and I go Saturday." She said it evenly, the way she delivered everything, as though she were an arbiter reading out a decision she had no part in making.

He sat down on the bench because his legs offered an opinion. All morning he had been organizing the day around Monday, around the two of them in the exam room, and now Monday rearranged itself without asking him.

"Then who's the video for," he said.

"For whoever finds it. For you, probably. You explain better to a camera than to me anyway." She nudged the tripod leg with her toe. "Finish it. Send me the link from Tucson. I want to watch you say introns again, it sounded like an insult."

He laughed, and it caught somewhere in his throat and came out wrong. He stood, checked the frame, and found Priya in the corner of it, sitting on the bench with the unmarked book, close enough that if he shifted the camera two degrees she would be in the shot for good. He didn't shift it. He pressed record instead, and said, "Transcription is where the copying starts," and behind him the creek carried the cut pieces away downstream.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
story:
Mr. Rowan had written one thing at the top of Victor's draft, in green ink that had bled through the page: What are you actually arguing? Victor had carried the paper around for three days before he could bring himself to open it again, and now it sat on the cafe table between his laptop and a cold cappuccino, the ink facing up like an accusation.

He was supposed to be fixing it. Instead he was rereading his own first sentence, the one he had been proud of: The Vietnam War ended in 1975. Below it, seven pages of dates and statistics and two footnotes copied carefully out of the style guide, and at the bottom, a bibliography with the commas in the right places, which had taken him most of a Sunday. None of that, apparently, mattered, because the top line said he hadn't argued anything at all.

"You look like your team lost," said Mara, dropping into the chair across from him with an iced tea. She had her own stack of work, an anatomy lab she was pretending not to have due tomorrow. She and Victor had maintained a cautious detente since the group project in November, when he had done all the slides and she had done all the talking, and both of them had sworn never to work together again. Studying at the same cafe was not working together. It was proximity.

"Rowan killed my draft," Victor said. He slid it across the table.

She read it while chewing her straw, and he watched her face do something complicated. "Your citations are really good," she offered.

"That's the worst part. I spent forever on the citations."

She turned to the first page again, tapped his opening sentence with one lacquered nail. "This is just true, though. Like, factually true. Nobody's going to fight you on it."

"That's what a paper is. Facts. You state the facts and you footnote them."

Mara pulled a battered green card out of her backpack, a handout from some class he wasn't in, and held it up. She read off it. "A thesis has to be arguable. A claim a reasonable person could dispute, not a fact everyone already accepts." She set the card down between them. "There's a whole rubric about it, apparently."

Victor looked at his seven pages. The war ended in 1975. He had built the whole thing on that, stacked dates on it like bricks, and a reasonable person could not dispute a single brick. He felt the ground shift a little, a small seismic event under something he had thought was solid, and what settled into the gap was a question he did not yet know how to answer: if the facts weren't the argument, what was?

"Okay," he said slowly. "So what would be arguable?"

"Something someone could say no to." Mara shrugged. "Like, I don't know, that the war ended the wrong way. That it should have ended sooner. That it changed something specific. That's yours to figure out, I have a fetal pig to label."

He opened a new document while she collated her lab diagrams into a pile and frowned at the arterial system. He typed a sentence and deleted it. Typed another. The war ended in 1975 was safe; nobody could tell him he was wrong. Every new sentence he drafted could be wrong, and that was the whole point, and it felt like standing at the edge of the high dive.

He tried: The way the war ended mattered more for Americans at home than for the Vietnamese. He stared at it. A reasonable person could dispute that. He could imagine his grandfather disputing it loudly, at Thanksgiving, with a napkin waved like a flag. That was somehow encouraging. But he also couldn't yet tell if it was something he could support with the sources he had, or whether he even believed it, and both of those uncertainties sat side by side without resolving into anything.

"Is this arguable?" he asked Mara, turning the laptop toward her.

She read it, squinted. "I'd fight you on it. So yes." She went back to her pig.

He started again, not from the first sentence this time but from the middle, from the one statistic he kept coming back to, about the number of veterans who came home in 1973, two years before the war itself ended. He had put it in a footnote before, a thing that sat in the margin. Now he moved it into the body of the paper and let a question grow out of it, and then a claim, tentative, half-formed, a sentence he could lose an argument over. He kept his old bibliography, since the sources were still sources, and added two new entries at the bottom, formatting them the way he had before, checking the commas.

The cafe had filled up around them. Mara closed her anatomy binder and stretched. "Did you solve your thesis problem?"

"Not solved," Victor said. "I have a sentence somebody could attack, and I don't know yet if I can defend it. I think that might be progress."

She laughed, and gathered her pens. At the door she paused and called back, "Good luck with Grandpa at Thanksgiving."

Victor looked down at the green ink at the top of his draft, then took out his pen and wrote beneath it, small but legible: Ask me now.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Sophie had been failing at chocolate for three Saturday afternoons, and she had begun to take it personally. The recipe said to melt the couverture to forty-five degrees, cool it to twenty-seven, then bring it back up to thirty-one and a half, and she had followed the numbers with the devotion of a girl who had once gotten a perfect score on a chemistry practical. What emerged from her friend Priya's kitchen each time was dull, soft, and streaked, chocolate with the personality of candle wax. Priya's little brother Dev lurked at the counter eating the failures anyway, which Sophie found both touching and demoralizing, like someone applauding at a funeral.

"Your problem," Priya said, stirring the bowl with the patience of someone who had watched this process four times, "is that you treat the thermometer like it's a judge. You keep waiting for it to tell you what to do."

"It is a judge. Tempering is just rules. Melt, cool, warm, hold. If I follow the rules it has to work."

Priya tapped the marble slab they had hauled from her mother's baking cupboard. "My grandmother never used a thermometer. She'd dab a little on her lip and know. Rules are the floor, not the ceiling." She said it so solemnly that Sophie laughed, and Priya said, "Write that down, it's an aphorism now, I get royalties."

Sophie did not write it down, but she did stop staring at the digital readout and start paying attention to the chocolate itself, the way it loosened as she stirred, the slight thickening when it was close. She spread a test layer on parchment with the edge of a spatula and pressed her palm against the back of it after a minute. It set. It looked, under the kitchen light, actually glossy, like something in a shop window. She shrieked in a register that brought Dev at a run.

They made thirty-two squares that afternoon, hazelnut and sea salt, and because Priya's mother wanted the counter cleared before her book club arrived, they slid the tray into the refrigerator to firm up fast. Sophie carried the parchment of extras to the living room, where Dev was already negotiating for two pieces, then three. The windows were open on an August evening, and the air coming in was thick enough to chew.

Twenty minutes later Dev held up a square and frowned at it. "Is this supposed to look like this?" The top of the chocolate had gone strange, a pale, dry dust across the dark surface, gritty when Sophie touched it with a fingertip, like someone had shaken powdered sugar over it while she wasn't looking. Her stomach dropped. She had tempered correctly, she was nearly sure of it, and yet here was the exact flaw she'd been fighting all along, arrived by some new route she couldn't see.

She did what she always did when confused: she called her aunt Reena, who was garrulous on any subject but never more so than on food, and put her on speaker while Dev, unable to wait for answers, ate a dusty square and pronounced it "fine, tastes the same, just feels weird, like sand on a beach that's made of chocolate."

"You chilled it and then took it out into the humid air, didn't you," Aunt Reena said, though it came out as a single long word, humidairdidn'tyou. "That's sugar bloom. The moisture in the room dissolves the sugar on the surface, and when it dries, the sugar recrystallizes, and there's your gritty white coating."

Priya watched Sophie's face as the sentence landed. In the two years they had been friends, Priya had learned to recognize this particular expression, the one that meant Sophie's whole model of the situation was quietly being taken apart and reassembled. It was the same look she'd had in tenth grade when the biology teacher told her that a tomato was a fruit. "So I did everything right," Sophie said slowly, "and then I broke it afterward. The tempering wasn't the problem. The fridge was."

"Then leave them out next time," Priya said. "Counter, cool corner, done."

But Sophie was staring at the tray, thumb rubbing a pale patch. "No, but which rules matter? The temperatures were rules, and they worked. The fridge was a rule I invented for speed. My grandmother-rule, your grandmother-rule, whatever. Rules are the floor, not the ceiling." She grinned. "Royalties accepted."

From the doorway, Priya's mother had been watching longer than either of them noticed, and she saw what Sophie could not: the girl standing in her living room in flour-dusted shorts, holding a ruined chocolate square up to the light like a jeweler with a flawed stone, turning it, almost delighted. "You know," Priya's mother said, "most people would have thrown the tray out by now."

Sophie looked over, considered the question underneath the remark, and was honest. "I don't know if I can fix these. They might just be like this." She set the square down on the parchment, where it sat pale and gritty among its glossy brothers, evidence of both things she now knew and the one thing she didn't. Dev reached past her and took it anyway.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
The bus shelter on Fifth Street still smelled of rain from the morning, though the sky had cleared into a washed, early-evening blue. Jackson sat on the bench with his permit folded into his back pocket, watching his mother's Corolla idle at the curb. His uncle Ray leaned out the passenger window. "You get one hour," he said. "Then I got to be back for my shift."

The hour was paid for, technically. Jackson had repaired Mrs. Okafor's laptop the week before, hunting down the malware that had eaten her tax files, and she had pressed an envelope into his hand afterward, calling it an honorarium, which he'd had to look up on the bus ride home. A payment for a service you weren't supposed to charge for. He'd decided the money was for driving lessons, since the community course was full until October and the test at the DMV was scheduled for the last Friday of August. College started three days later.

They started in the empty lot behind the Aldi, where someone had lined up two traffic cones exactly the length of a parked car and a half. "Parallel parking is geometry," Uncle Ray said, chewing a toothpick. "The highway is judgment. Different animal entirely." Jackson practiced the geometry first: reverse, crank the wheel, watch the cone in the mirror until it vanished, crank back. He clipped the rear cone four times, then five, and on the sixth try the Corolla slid into the space with a foot to spare on each side. His hands were shaking anyway. "See, you're proving something to the examiner you already proved to the cones," Ray said. "Now comes the part that's harder to teach."

The on-ramp to Route 9 rose ahead of them, and Jackson's throat went tight the way it did before exams. He merged too slow the first time, a pickup honking as it swung around him, and Ray said nothing, which was worse than shouting. The second ramp, Jackson accelerated hard and slipped into a gap between a box truck and a sedan, and for a moment the car was simply part of the traffic, one thread in a moving weave. He let out a breath. "That's it," Ray said. "That's exactly it."

But ten minutes in, following the box truck, Jackson realized he was close enough to count the rivets on its back doors. He'd acclimated to the speed, his body had stopped panicking and started to feel comfortable, and comfort had shortened the distance without his noticing. "You're riding him," Ray said. "Tell me what you know about following distance."

Jackson searched his memory of the driver's manual, read in fragments on the bus, and found one clear thing. "You keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead," he said. "A longer gap in rain, snow or darkness." Ray nodded once. "So prove it. Watch the shoulder. When his back bumper passes a sign, count."

A green mile marker slid under the truck's shadow. "One one-thousand, two one-thousand." Jackson's front bumper hadn't reached the marker yet, but barely. He eased off the gas until the next marker gave him a full count, and the third marker a little more, because the sun was lowering and the light on the asphalt had turned the color of weak tea, and he wanted the margin the manual promised for darkness. The truck pulled away ahead of him. Nobody honked. Nothing happened at all, which felt like the strangest kind of victory.

Driving home in the blue hour, Jackson held the count at every sign, and he found himself thinking that the two rules he'd learned that evening argued with each other. Merging demanded aggression, a decision made in half a second and committed to fully; following demanded restraint, a patience held open for the sake of a stranger's brake lights. He couldn't decide yet whether good driving meant choosing between them or holding both at once, the way his mother could argue a position fiercely and still change her mind later. Maybe the examiner would ask. Maybe nobody would ever ask, and he'd have to work it out alone over years of highways.

Ray had him parallel park one final time outside the house, between the mailbox and the hydrant, and the Corolla settled into the space clean on the first try. "Same time Thursday," Ray said, gathering his jacket. "You're paying for the gas this month, remember." Jackson grinned and turned off the engine, then turned it back on, just to hear it, then turned it off again and pocketed the keys.
