activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Charlotte arrived at the Saturday market before seven, when the vendors were still unbrellas-ing their awnings and the grass in the courthouse lawn was wet enough to soak through her sneakers. She carried a plastic tub of truffles she had made the night before, and the problem was visible from the moment she lifted the lid: every one of them had gone dull, a gray bloom spread across the tops like frost on a window. She had made them for Mrs. Okafor, who kept the chocolate stall at the end of the row and who had said, twice now, that if Charlotte ever produced a batch that snapped cleanly, she could sell them on commission.

Mrs. Okafor picked up a truffle without greeting her. She turned it under the light of the stall lamp, pressed her thumbnail into the shell, and watched it give like candle wax instead of breaking. "The chocolate wasn't in temper," she said. "It set wrong, so the fat came to the surface. Taste it." Charlotte tasted it. It was fine and it was also wrong, waxy on the tongue, and she said so.

"Come around," Mrs. Okafor said. On the counter behind the cash box sat a slab of pale stone, and Charlotte recognized it from the kitchen of her friend Priya, whose mother did all her pastry work on a cold stone counter and yelled at anyone who set a hot pan on it. Mrs. Okafor melted a bowl of dark chocolate over a pan of barely simmering water, then poured a third of it onto the slab and began working it with a spatula, spreading it out and scraping it back, spreading and scraping, the pool narrowing and thickening and losing its shine.

"What are you doing?" Charlotte asked.

"Tabling," Mrs. Okafor said. She kept spreading and working the chocolate on the cool slab to bring its temperature down and start stable crystals forming, and she said it the way someone says a word they've said ten thousand times, without pausing. "You spread it thin, you gather it up, you spread it again. Watch the edges. When they start to set, it's telling you something."

Charlotte had read about tempering the way she read about most things, which was quickly and with a plan to figure out the rest later. The internet had given her temperatures and a seeding method involving chopped chocolate stirred in off the heat, and she had followed it with a thermometer she now suspected was off by several degrees. Priya's mother had once offered the stone counter for exactly this purpose, and Charlotte had declined because the seeding method had seemed cleaner, less like work, more like a recipe. She was honest enough with herself to admit that she had wanted the shortcut to be the real method.

Mrs. Okafor pulled the pooled chocolate back into the warm bowl, stirred, and poured again, and the chocolate on the slab now moved differently, thicker, holding a ridge when the spatula lifted. "Your hands," she said, and put the spatula in Charlotte's grip. The stone was colder than Charlotte expected, cold enough that she felt it through the handle, and the chocolate stiffened at the edges faster than she had judged it would. Her first pass was too slow and a strip of it set solid in a dull streak. Mrs. Okafor scraped it back into the mass without comment.

Charlotte spread and gathered, spread and gathered. The motion was repetitive in the way that had always made her impatient, but she found she could not think about anything else while doing it, which was its own kind of relief. The market was filling behind her, a woman arguing in a bellicose voice about the price of heirloom tomatoes two stalls down, a busker tuning a fiddle, and none of it reached her. She worked the chocolate until it thickened against the stone, and Mrs. Okafor dipped a knife point in, let it set for ten seconds, and broke it off. The snap was small and clean, like a knuckle cracking.

"Your turn, all of it," Mrs. Okafor said, and stepped back from the counter entirely. Charlotte melted a fresh batch, poured a third onto the slab, and began. She ruined the first attempt by scraping too hard and breaking the mass into grains; she recovered it by warming it back into the bowl and starting over. On the second attempt she watched the edges the way she had been shown, and when the chocolate held its ridges, she moved fast, folding it back into the warm bowl before it could over-set. She dipped the truffles from the night before, remade in fresh shells, and set them on parchment in the shade of the awning.

While they set, she and Mrs. Okafor sat on the crates behind the stall and split a wedge of bread from the baker three rows over. Charlotte thought about calling Priya's mother, or not calling, and about the fact that she had refused a good offer because it looked like the harder road, and how the harder road and the real one had turned out to be the same road, though she couldn't have known that in advance and still wasn't sure the analogy held everywhere it seemed to. There was probably a version of this that was only about chocolate. She ate her bread and let it be undecided.

After twenty minutes Mrs. Okafor picked up a finished truffle, held it to the lamp, and turned it. The shell was dark and glossy, throwing a clean line of light. She broke it in half and handed half to Charlotte, who put it in her mouth and bit down.

story:
The newspaper arrived on Tuesdays, folded into a plastic sleeve that smelled faintly of the newsagent's shop two streets over, and it was written entirely in Arabic. Alexis had volunteered to read it aloud before he understood what that would mean. His grandfather's eyes had been failing since the spring, and the radio only gave headlines, so the old man wanted the whole article, the one about water rights, read to him after lunch. Alexis had said yes because saying no felt like a small betrayal, and because he assumed his Arabic was good enough.

It was good enough for the kitchen. He had spent every summer of his childhood in this house, and his grandfather's dialect came to him as easily as the smell of cardamom. He could argue about football, could ask for the good bread, could joke. On the video calls during the school year his mother said his accent had inured itself to the rhythm of the old man's speech, so that on the phone people sometimes mistook Alexis for a cousin. That was the Arabic he had. It was not, he discovered on the first Tuesday, the Arabic on the page.

He sat at the table with the paper propped against the sugar bowl and began, and within a sentence he was lost. The words had the look of words he knew, the same looping letters, but they behaved strangely, sitting in orders his mouth didn't expect, wearing endings he had never heard his grandfather use. He stopped and started three times. His grandfather said nothing, only turned his teacup slowly on its saucer, and Alexis felt the silence lean on him.

"Say it again," his grandfather said at last. "Slower."

"I don't know some of these words." It was a confession Alexis hadn't planned to make. "They're like... they're the right letters but wrong everything else."

His grandfather laughed, a short dry sound, and tapped the table with two fingers. "The newspaper is written in Modern Standard Arabic," he said. "Not the way we talk. All the papers write it like that, and not only here. In Egypt, in Morocco, the same writing. One newspaper voice, and every reader in every country reads it." He shrugged, as if this were the least remarkable thing in the world, and Alexis sat very still with the feeling of a door opening sideways instead of forward. A thousand spoken Arabics, and behind them one written language, like a wall behind a row of separate gardens. He had never suspected the wall.

The problem was still the problem, though. He had promised to read the article, and he could not read it. His first instinct was to translate honestly, word by broken word, and hope the gaps would be forgivable. His second instinct, which arrived faster and more seductively, was to guess. He knew what water-rights articles generally said; he could improvise something in the dialect, fluent and warm, and his grandfather, who could not see the page, would never know. For a moment this seemed almost kind. Then it seemed like relativism dressed up as kindness, the belief that a comfortable story was as good as a true one because the listener would feel the same either way. His grandfather had spent forty years reading this paper and disagreeing with it loudly. He deserved the actual article, not Alexis's invention.

So Alexis changed the method. He went through the piece sentence by sentence with a battered dictionary from the hall shelf, and where a word resisted him he wrote it in the margin and moved on. His grandfather drank tea and waited with a patience that seemed, for once, not entirely calm. Something in the way he kept glancing toward the window made Alexis slow down and pay attention to the paper itself, and only then, in the third column, did he see the dateline and the name of the town. It was his grandfather's town. The one he'd left at nineteen and never returned to. The article was not a general piece about water rights at all; it was about the valley he had grown up in, where the springs were low this year.

Alexis read the sentence twice in his head before saying anything. His voice, when he used it, was careful. "Jiddo. It's about your valley." The old man's hand stopped on the saucer. "The springs there," Alexis went on, navigating the strange formal shapes, and now the effort of decoding felt different, urgent rather than academic, because the man across the table had suddenly become a boy from that valley listening for news of home.

The reading was still imperfect. Alexis stumbled on the long constructed words, and when his grandfather corrected him the corrections came in the dialect, a translation back into the kitchen language, and Alexis began to notice the two systems running side by side, the formal one on the page and the living one at the table, each one carrying something the other couldn't. He did the summary at the end as he'd been asked, aloud, in his own words, halting between registers, and the summary was honest about its own gaps: "That's most of it," he said. "I think I got the numbers right. I'm not sure what the minister actually promised. It's equivocal, the way he says it."

"The way they all say it," his grandfather said.

They sat afterward while the light moved across the oilcloth. Alexis could not tell whether the news was good or bad for the town, whether the springs being low meant a bad year or only a difficult one, and he said so, and his grandfather nodded as though the uncertainty were the truest part of the whole exercise. He asked whether the paper would come next Tuesday, and Alexis said it would, and then he got up and rinsed the teacups and set them upside down on the rack, the way he had been shown, the water running briefly loud in the quiet kitchen.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
story:
Olivier taped the prompt to the wall above the desk: a ten-minute play drawn from your own life, staged in the living room for family, due Sunday. He had a subject already, the afternoon his father missed his regional swim final because a client's deposition ran long, and Olivier had swum the race alone in a lane with no one he knew watching. He opened a blank document and wrote three lines of dialogue between a boy and a mother in a car. It read like a transcript of nothing.

His sister Colette came in without knocking, holding a bag of frozen peas against her elbow. She had volleyball tryouts Monday and had decided the living room stage meant casting. "I want a part," she said. "I'm not doing your play about swimming with no girls in it."

"There are girls. Mom's in it."

"Mom has four lines and you know it." She dropped onto the bed and read his pages over his shoulder, which he hated. "This is just people talking in a car. Where's the play part?"

He didn't have an answer. After she left he sat with the anthology from his mother's shelf, the one she'd used in college, because he remembered a play in it where someone stood outside the story and talked to the audience. He found it near the back. The Glass Menagerie. Tennessee Williams called it a memory play, and the introduction noted it was first staged in Chicago in 1944, narrated by Tom, who looks back on his family. Olivier read the opening page twice, then the stage direction about the narrator stepping to the edge of the stage. Tom wasn't in the scene and was in the scene at once. That was the play part.

He restructured everything that night at the kitchen table. A narrator named Olivier would walk out in his own clothes, past the mother and the boy he was playing, and tell the audience what he could not have known at the time: that his father had sat in a parking garage afterward, that the deposition had been for a case he would lose. The older Olivier could say things the younger one could only swim through. It solved the problem of the car, which had been static, and it created a new one. If the narrator was him, then everything on stage was his arrangement of the past, and he could arrange it however he wanted. He could make the father's absence mean neglect, or make it mean nothing, and the audience would take whichever he chose. He had thought a play about himself would be simple because he already knew all the facts. It turned out the facts were the easy part.

Colette read the new draft at breakfast and gave it back slowly, which from her was approval. "Okay, this is actually a play," she said. "I'll do the narrator if you're being the boy. You can't do both, it's weird." She wanted the walk to the edge of the stage; he could see her practicing it in the hallway mirror later, one hand flat against the frame, deciding how to stand. He told her the narrator should be him because the whole idea was that it was his memory. She said, "So it's a memory play, like the glass animal one," and he said yes, and she said the narrator should still be a girl, because a sister remembering her brother's race was the same event from the better angle, and he made her stop talking because he was starting to agree.

He tried her way for a day. Colette as the narrator gave the piece a second perspective, someone whose memory of the parking garage differed from his, and it complicated the play in a direction he liked. But it also felt like chicanery, a trick to hand the best role to a person who happened to live down the hall, and he couldn't tell whether that was a real objection or a parochial one, a defense of his small territory. His mother, when he asked her over dinner which version was truer, said, "Which one do you want to watch?" and went back to her soup.

Sunday afternoon he taped a rectangle of floor in the living room and set six folding chairs. His father sat in the middle row with his coat still on. Olivier had spent Saturday trying to parametrize the choice, listing what each narrator version gained and lost like variables in a model, and had ended by closing the notebook, because the list made both versions identical on paper and he still preferred one. He stepped to the tape. Colette stood just off the rectangle, holding the script in case he failed, which he had told her not to do and she had agreed to do anyway.

The house lights, such as they were, stayed on, because this was a living room and not the Lyceum, as Colette had pointed out when he asked for the dimmer switch. Olivier stood at the edge of the tape, looked at the folding chairs, at his father's hands folded on his knees, and began.

"I'll tell you what I knew then, and after, I'll tell you what I found out."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
story:
Jake's mother had left on Tuesday for a two-week course in Milwaukee, and the note on the fridge said, in her handwriting that always leaned right under pressure: "You cook now. Budget's in the tin." His father could boil pasta and call it a night, but the tin held eighty dollars in fives, and the note's last line said it had to last. So on Saturday morning Jake found himself at the farmers' market on River Street with a list he had written the night before, a list that read, in full: chicken, rice, beans, something green, oats.

The list was his own idea, sort of. His older cousin Dana had emailed him a plan, four dinners cooked Sunday in batches and reheated all week, and Jake had printed it and then felt the strange weight of a printed document in a house where nobody printed anything. Dana's plan assumed a grocery store. The market was where his mother shopped, though, and the eighty dollars was hers, so it seemed right to start there.

He bought a whole chicken from a man in a canvas hat who wrapped it in butcher paper and said, "Three and a half pounds, best bird here," and Jake said, "Okay," because he had no other information to offer. At the next stall a woman sold greens in rubber-banded bunches, and past her a fish vendor had a hand-lettered sign reading LITTORAL CATCH, with mackerel laid out on ice like silver bars. He bought the greens. He stood in front of the mackerel for a while, doing a kind of math that had no numbers in it yet, and moved on.

The oats were the problem. His mother bought oats somewhere, and the container at home had about a bowl left in it. The market had a bulk stall with big jars, but beside it a table held packaged bags, and one bag was enormous, the size of a pillow, labeled VALUE SIZE. Jake picked it up. It was heavy and it seemed obvious that big meant cheap, the way his grandfather bought mayonnaise in tubs. The stall's owner, a teenager about his own age with a laminated price sheet taped to the table, was weighing someone's almonds.

Jake looked at the shelf labels. Under each bag there was a small white tag, and on the tag, below the price, was a second number. The pillow bag cost more than the small bag but the second number, printed smaller, was higher too. He read both tags twice. He did the thing where you pretend to be casually reading while actually not understanding anything at all.

"What's that bottom number?" he asked the teenager.

"Unit price," she said. "Cost per gram. It's on everything."

He looked at the rice bags, and there it was again, and on the oils, which were sold by the litre, and on the eggs, priced per item. The small bag of oats had the lower one. He set the pillow bag down with the care of a man defusing something, and bought the small bag, and the whole shelf seemed to rearrange itself in his head, every package suddenly declaring what it actually cost.

At home he exhumed his mother's biggest pot from the cabinet above the stove, the one buried behind the colander, and roasted the chicken, and while it rested he cooked the rice in the pot and the beans in a smaller one. Dana's plan called for dividing everything into containers, which they had, and for labeling them with days, which felt absurd until Sunday night when he stood in the kitchen eating reheated chicken and rice off a real plate and thought, with some amazement, that Tuesday's dinner already existed, was already cooked and waiting, and that he had made it so.

His father drifted through around eight and looked in the fridge at the stacked containers. "This is a lot of food."

"It's the week," Jake said. "One cooking day, five dinners. It's cheaper per meal, I did the math."

His father took a container out, examined the lid, and put it back. "There's leftover pad thai in here from before your mom left."

"Throw it out," Jake said. "There's no amnesty for that. It's from another era."

By Thursday the plan had held, mostly. The greens had gone limp a day early, which nobody had warned him about, and he'd eaten the chicken down to a frame that he boiled for stock because Dana's email said to and because it seemed wasteful not to. The oats were fine. What he couldn't stop thinking was how he'd nearly carried the pillow bag to the register, certain of a bargain that wasn't there, and how many other things he was probably certain about that weren't there either. He didn't have an answer for that. He had Friday's dinner, still sitting in its container with his handwriting on the lid, and he took it out and put it on a plate.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
Sadie spread the photocopied chapter across the kitchen table and set a mug at each corner to keep the pages flat, because the summer reading packet had arrived curled like something left in a car window. The assignment said to apply a critical lens to one chapter, either feminist or Marxist, and to write two pages by Friday. She had picked Jane Eyre because she loved it, which she was already beginning to suspect was a mistake.

Her mother came through with a basket of laundry balanced on one hip and paused long enough to read the top page upside down. "That's the wedding chapter," she said. "The one where it all falls apart."

"That's the one." Sadie slid the basket's weight toward her mother's free hand without thinking about it, steadying the towels that had begun to slip. "I have to ruin it with theory now."

Her mother laughed and carried the basket toward the stairs. "Ruin it gently, then."

Sadie started with the feminist lens because it felt obvious. Rochester dressed as a gypsy to extract confessions; Jane was expected to feel and not to be felt for; the whole machinery of the scene ran on a woman being deceived by a man who controlled the house she lived in. She wrote a paragraph and read it back and it was fine, it was even good, but it sounded like something a savant would produce, brilliant and bloodless, a list of observations nobody had asked her to care about. She underlined it anyway.

It was while flipping back to check a quotation that she noticed the footman. He appeared twice in the chapter: once to admit a stranger, once to carry a note. He had no name. Neither did the maid who packed Jane's trunk in the middle of the crisis, working while Jane wept, or the coachman who would drive her away into the moor night. Sadie sat with her pen stopped on the page. Somebody had packed that trunk. Somebody had lit the candles Jane saw by, and cooked the meal nobody in the drawing room finished, and would sweep up the wedding that never happened. She went through the chapter with a ruler and made a small tally in the margin: how many times servants appeared, and how many times any of them spoke. The gap was so wide it looked like a typo.

She texted Dev, who was doing the same assignment across town. Did you count the servants. He replied three minutes later with a photo of his own margins, tallied in green ink, and the message: mine never talk either. Then: is that the marxist thing? whose labour pays for the tea party?

Sadie wrote at the top of a fresh page: A Marxist reading asks whose labour makes these lives possible. Then she stopped, because the sentence had a trenchant edge she hadn't earned yet, and she went back to the chapter to earn it. The strange thing was that the lens didn't desiccate the book the way she'd feared. It made the house louder. Every scene now had people in the walls, and the romance that had made her cry at fourteen was suddenly standing on somebody else's bent back, and both things were still true at once, which was the part her draft couldn't hold yet.

Her mother came down in her reading glasses and set a plate of toast beside the tallies. "You've been at this for hours."

"I found the servants," Sadie said.

"In Jane Eyre?"

"In the walls of Jane Eyre." She turned the margin toward her mother, the green counts and the little hatch marks, and explained it in one breath: the comfort on the page was built by people the book mentions only in passing, and once you counted them you couldn't stop. Her mother pulled out the opposite chair and sat down, which she almost never did at this hour, and read the tallies through the bottom of her glasses.

"That's the trunk scene," she said, tapping a line. "The maid packing while Jane stands there. I never once thought about her." She looked up. "So which lens are you going to write about, the women or the workers?"

Sadie turned her pen over in her fingers. The feminist paragraph sat on the left page, the tallies on the right, and between them the chapter that had produced both. "I don't think they're separate," she said. "Jane has almost nothing, but she still has someone packing her trunk for her. I don't know what to do with that yet."

"You have until Friday," her mother said, and pushed the plate closer, and took one piece of toast for herself.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
story:
The bookshop on Mercer Street ran its Thursday night reading group in the back, between the poetry shelf and a radiator that clanked like a small industry. Brianna had come the first time because her English teacher mentioned it in passing and left a folded flyer on her desk, and she kept coming because the chairs were ugly and nobody cared what she wore. Tonight the table held eleven copies of Pride and Prejudice, a plate of biscotti someone had bought at the closing bakery, and a printed page with a single paragraph from chapter twenty, the one where Elizabeth turns down Mr Collins.

She had read the novel twice before college started, once for speed and once for the sentences. She had never read it the way Dana from the group read it, which was slowly and with a pencil, as though the book were a machine with a panel she intended to open. Dana was twenty-six and worked at the courthouse and said things like "the marriage market is the only market these women are allowed to trade in," and Brianna wrote that down, then felt embarrassed at having written it down, then kept the note anyway.

"Read it again," Dana said, tapping the paragraph, "and ask who owns what."

"Elizabeth owns nothing," Brianna said. "That's why it's romantic. She gives up security for love."

"Is that why it's romantic? Or is that the story we've agreed to tell about it?"

Mrs Adeyemi, who owned the shop and paid the group's guest speaker a small honorarium out of the register, leaned forward on her stool. She had grown up in a house her brother inherited, and she did not say this often, but she said it now. "Before anyone falls in love with Elizabeth's freedom, you should know the practical fact underneath this whole book. The Bennet estate is entailed to a male heir, Mr Collins. So none of the five Bennet daughters can inherit their father's home."

The radiator clanked twice, and everyone let the sentence sit. Brianna looked down at the paragraph on her page, where Mr Collins was proposing, and saw it differently, the way a street looks different once you learn it used to be a riverbed.

"So when Mrs Bennet pushes the girls at rich men," said Tomas, a sophomore who ate biscotti like he was being timed, "she's not just silly. She's the only one doing financial planning in the house."

"She's the one who can see the cliff," Dana said.

Brianna turned her pencil over. She had spent years disliking Mrs Bennet on Austen's instructions, and now she was being asked to notice that the author's mockery might itself be a lens, one that had been fitted to the book before she ever opened it. She tried to hold both ideas at once, the way you hold two lenses up to the same window. Through one, the entail was the pressure that made every proposal a matter of survival, marriage as the daughters' only route to a roof. Through the other, the comedy depended on treating the women who felt that pressure most keenly as jokes. She wondered whether the book could know the first thing and still do the second, whether that was contradiction or just the ground it stood on.

"What if you parametrize it," she said slowly, not sure the word belonged in a sentence spoken aloud. "Like, vary the money. If the Bennets were rich, none of this happens. If the daughters could inherit, none of this happens. The whole plot moves on one legal fact."

"Entail," said Mrs Adeyemi. "That's the word for it. Everything follows from that."

Dana grinned at her. "That's a Marxist reading and a feminist reading holding hands. Careful. People get tectonic about that."

The conversation went on past closing time, through Charlotte Lucas marrying for a house and the question of whether Elizabeth's final happiness was freedom or simply the best available cage. Brianna argued, then conceded a point, then argued it back. What she could not settle, even walking home under the yellow streetlights with the photocopy folded in her jacket, was whether Austen had criticized the world of the entail or only described it with such precision that criticism became possible later, by readers with lenses Austen never held. Maybe both. Maybe that was the tectonic thing, two readings grinding against each other somewhere under the surface, and the reader standing on top feeling only a faint tremor and calling it delight.

She stopped at the corner to text her mother, who had been after her all summer to be practical about college. You'd like this book, she typed. This girl's whole future comes down to property law. Her mother replied before she reached the next block: See, that's what I keep telling you. Read something romantic and it's still about money in the end. You should meet my friend's son, he's studying real estate.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
story:
Clara had run the school loop every day for three weeks, and on Thursday she was eleven seconds slower than she had been on the first Monday. She stood at the fence with her hands on her knees, watching Priya jog the cooldown lane beside the field, and she did not say anything, because saying it would make it true in front of someone else.

"Your splits were better in February," Priya said when she came over. "And you weren't training then."

"I'm getting worse by trying harder. That's not supposed to be how it works."

"It isn't," Priya said, and Clara heard the small cruelty of accuracy in it, though Priya meant it kindly.

That night Clara sat on her bedroom floor with her laptop and a notebook, typing phrases like why am I slower when I train every day. Most of what came back was junk, forums full of disaffected former athletes complaining about their coaches, maligning rest days as an invention of lazy people. She almost closed the laptop. But one thread had a word she kept circling back to, a word she'd never heard anyone at school say, and she copied it into her notebook with a line under it: supercompensation.

She found it again in a chapter of an old training manual the library kept behind the desk, a book nobody had signed out since before she was born. The idea was strange at first, almost revisionist, like being told you had been reading a sentence backwards your whole life. The fitness came after. The body rebuilt itself beyond where it had been, but only in the quiet days between. The workout itself was the tearing down; the repair was where you got faster. She read the page three times, then closed the book and looked at the wall. Every day she had trained, she had given herself no quiet days at all. No rebuilding. Just tearing.

On Monday she taped a sheet of paper inside her locker door. Hard intervals Tuesday. Easy Friday. Nothing Sunday, which felt like a small betrayal, like leaving a word out of a sentence on purpose. Warm-ups first, ten minutes of jogging and drills she'd always skipped as a waste of time. She told Priya about it at lunch, keeping her voice low so the table wouldn't hear.

"So I run hard," Clara said, "and then I rest, and the resting is where it happens."

"The resting is where you get fitter," Priya said. "It's called supercompensation."

"That's the word." Clara turned her water bottle in her hands. "The thing I can't tell is whether one day is enough. Or whether I'm just making an excuse to do less."

"You'll find out Thursday."

Thursday came cold and gray, the track damp from morning rain. Clara did the drills first, the boring ones, high knees and skipping, feeling faintly ridiculous while the boys' team watched from the shed. Then the 400s. On the first one her legs were heavy and she thought, there it is, the same wall. But by the third interval something had loosened, and on the fourth she came through the back straight faster than she had in any of the three weeks before. She crossed the line and heard Priya calling her split from the fence.

"Faster than February," Priya shouted.

Clara walked a slow curve, breathing hard, not letting herself decide yet what it meant. One good day could be sleep, or weather, or nothing. She would have to run the whole week again, and the week after, and rest on Sunday again, and write down every number, and only then would she know. She bent and retied her shoe, pulling the knot tight twice.

"Same plan Monday," she said. "Sunday stays empty."

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
story:
The waiting room of the Cedar Hollow Animal Clinic smelled of iodine and damp dog, and Logan had claimed the corner chair beside the fish tank because it had the only outlet for his phone charger. His biology final was in two days. On his lap, a review sheet covered in his own handwriting, arrows marching across the page: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain, glucose breaking down in the mitochondria until the cell walked away with ATP. He could recite the steps. He could not yet see them.

His mother was at the front desk with Mr. Abara, whose shepherd mix, Rukus, had been coughing since Tuesday. Through the half-open door to exam room two, Logan could hear Dr. Patel's voice, low and unhurried, and then the sound of a dog panting, quick and shallow, like something being counted.

"You're the one who wants to be a vet," said a girl across the room. She was maybe his age, a cat carrier on the seat beside her, a spiral notebook she'd been drawing in pushed facedown on her knees.

"Maybe," Logan said. "I volunteer here Saturdays. Today I'm just the ride for my mom."

She nodded at his review sheet. "Respiration? I did that last year. It looks like a subway map."

"That's my problem. I know the stops, not the train." He turned the page toward her. "Like, okay, the whole thing, the big picture, glucose plus six oxygen molecules gives you six carbon dioxide, six water, and energy. I can write that. But I don't understand what the dog is actually doing with it."

The girl, whose name turned out to be Priya, tilted her head. "Breathing, basically. That's the whole thing."

"Breathing isn't respiration," Logan said, and then heard how it sounded, and softened it. "My teacher would kill me if I got that wrong on the final. Respiration is the chemistry in the cells. Breathing is just moving the air in and out."

From the exam room, Rukus's panting rose again, and Logan found himself listening differently. In went oxygen, out came carbon dioxide, and somewhere between, in the mitochondria of every cell in that dog's heaving chest, glucose was being taken apart. Six oxygen molecules for every one glucose. Six carbon dioxide back out, six water, and energy the cells could spend. Rukus wasn't just hot. He was running the equation, millions of times a second, and his body was hauling away the exhaust.

Mr. Abara came out first, rubbing his eyes with the heel of his hand, and Mrs. Linh from the desk brought him a cup of water without his asking. Dr. Patel followed, clipboard against her hip, and Logan stood up without deciding to.

"Is he okay?"

"Congestive, probably. We're running bloodwork." She looked at him the way she did on Saturdays, like he was staff who happened to be sixteen. "You want to see how we draw it? Watch his oxygen sats?"

He glanced at his mother, who waved him off, and followed Dr. Patel into the room, review sheet still in his hand.

Rukus lay on the steel table, flanks working. A clip on his tongue, a wire to a small monitor. "Ninety-one percent," Dr. Patel said. "Not great, not catastrophic." She tapped the screen. "He's not getting oxygen where he needs it. You know where he needs it?"

Logan looked at the number, at the dog, at the arrows on his own page. "The mitochondria," he said. "The oxygen ends up in the mitochondria. That's where glucose gets broken down. That's where the energy comes from."

Dr. Patel raised an eyebrow, not quite smiling. "Somebody's studying."

"Final on Thursday." He set the review sheet on the counter, and while she positioned the needle for the blood draw, he steadied Rukus's leg the way she'd taught him last summer, palm flat, pressure gentle. The dog's panting fogged the steel. Logan counted breaths without meaning to and did the arithmetic in the margin of his notes: each exhale carrying carbon out of this body, carbon that had entered as glucose in Mr. Abara's kitchen, in kibble, in whatever lineage of meals had led to this animal on this table. The carbon in the dog's breath had been sugar an hour ago. The whole tectonic weight of biochemistry was happening under his palm, and it was warm, and it was fragile.

"He's a good one," Dr. Patel said quietly, because Rukus had flinched and then gone still under Logan's hand. "Some of them fight. He trusts."

Later, in the waiting room, Priya was gone, and on the chair she'd left her notebook open, folded to a page where she'd drawn the whole cycle as a subway map after all, stations and transfers, water and carbon dioxide labeled at the exits. Her cat's name was written at the top: Biscuit. Logan photographed the page, then closed the notebook and gave it to Mrs. Linh at the desk, in case Priya came back.

His mother came out signing a form, mouth tight. "They want to keep him overnight," she said. "I told Mr. Abara we'd wait and drive him home."

So they waited, and Logan sat with his review sheet, and every few minutes the door to the back opened, and he could hear Rukus breathing.

"Ninety-three," a technician called through the doorway, to nobody in particular.

Logan wrote it at the bottom of the page, under the arrows: 93. Then, beneath that, glucose plus six oxygen, six carbon dioxide and six water and energy, going in and going out of one dog all night, and he underlined it once and put his pen away.

story:
The assignment had seemed simple until Daniel read it a third time. Choose two scholarly articles on the same question, compare their arguments, and render a verdict: which made the better case, and why. He had picked the first article in ten minutes, a study from a psychology journal on whether sleep deprivation affected moral judgment in adolescents. Finding the second had taken two evenings of searching, and the winner was a paper whose results contradicted the first one almost point for point. He printed both and spread them across the library table like a duelist arranging pistols.

The trouble began with a citation check. Daniel was halfway through his notes when he noticed that his second article, the one he privately favored because it was better written, listed no journal anywhere on its pages. No volume number, no issue, no masthead. Just a repository name, a long string of letters and digits, and a green banner across the first page that read "PREPRINT." He sat back. Ms. Okonkwo had spent one afternoon in September warning the class about sources, and he had spent that afternoon drawing sharks in his margin.

He carried the paper to Priya's table, where she was highlighting something with the insouciant calm of a person who had finished her own review two days early. "Look at this," he said, tapping the banner. "It says preprint. Is that like a draft?"

Priya pulled the page toward her and squinted. "My cousin works at a lab. A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review." She slid it back. "So its findings haven't been checked yet."

"Checked by who?"

"Independent experts. The ones a journal picks." She returned to her highlighting, apparently considering the matter closed, which for her it was.

Daniel stood there a moment, holding the paper as if it might be radioactive, or as if it might not be, and the not-knowing was the problem. He carried it back to his table and read the methods section again, slowly, the way you look at a bridge after learning no engineer had signed off on it. The study was larger than the first one. The statistical analysis was more thorough, or at least longer. The prose was sharper. Every quality that had made him prefer it was still sitting there on the page, unimpressed by his new doubt.

At home he tried drafting anyway. The first paragraph came out confident and dishonest, weighing the two articles as if they were identical coins, and he deleted it after two sentences because writing it felt like a small act of mendacity he would have to keep paying for. He tried the opposite approach, dismissing the preprint entirely, and that draft collapsed even faster; the article's argument was better, and pretending otherwise made his own reasoning worse. His cat watched him type and delete from the desk chair she had confiscated, and offered no position on the epistemology of unpublished science.

The next morning he cornered Priya by the vending machines. "So if the findings haven't been checked by experts the journal chose, is the whole paper garbage, or is it just... pending?"

"Pending," Priya said. "That's why the journal version matters when it comes out. Sometimes they change."

"Sometimes they don't."

"Sometimes they don't," she agreed, and bought her chips.

In study hall, Daniel spread both articles out one last time and made a column on the back of his Spanish worksheet. On one side he wrote what the journal article had going for it: it had survived review, which meant experts chosen by the journal had checked it, whatever else that was worth. On the other side he wrote what the preprint had: a bigger sample, a clearer method, an argument that actually addressed its own weaknesses instead of papering over them. Then, at the bottom, he wrote a sentence he did not delete: the second article was probably right, and he could not yet prove it was, and both of those things could be true at once. He read it over. It looked strange on the page, like a receipt for something he hadn't bought yet.

When Ms. Okonkwo circulated the room and paused at his desk, he gesticulated at the two papers with his pen, covering the preprint and uncovering it again, as though the gesture itself were an argument. "I want to say the unpublished one is stronger," he told her. "But I also want to say I trust it less. Can I do both?"

She looked at his worksheet, at the column, at the sentence at the bottom, and gave him the particular smile she reserved for questions she had no intention of answering. "That's what the review is for," she said, and moved on down the row. Daniel looked at his blank first page, then at the green banner, then out the window at the parking lot, where somebody's balloon had escaped and was rising past the gymnasium, unreviewed, into the open air.
